pure-announcement.rationale: It is an evidence review of what llms.txt actually does, not a launch or release note, despite ending with the author's product plug.

duplicate.rationale: The corpus has no llms.txt concept (the rubric's exemplar is canned text, and a grep of concepts/ confirms none), and the supplied nearest concepts are all unrelated agent/retrieval topics.

unfalsifiable.rationale: Its central claims cite Google's own June 2026 Search Central docs and four named measurement studies (SE Ranking, Ahrefs, Limy, Otterly) with linked sources and sample sizes.

durability.rationale: The rubric's own weak exemplar is llms.txt for exactly this reason: the claims rest on dated adoption and fetch statistics and on vendor postures (Google Search vs Chrome Lighthouse) that the article itself concedes could flip if agentic browsing grows.

actionability.rationale: It ends in a concrete decision rule — ship the file as half-day agent-readiness infrastructure if developers-in-agents are your audience, and never treat it as a ranking or GEO lever — which directly changes what a site owner does.

atomicity.rationale: The whole article supports one statable idea: llms.txt has no measured effect on search or AI citations and its only real consumers are coding agents and agentic browsers.
